title: Getting the Love You Want
author: Harville Hendrix
theme: The struggles of a committed relationship are not a sign of failure but an invitation to heal old childhood hurts, and couples who learn to listen and change for each other can grow a conscious, lasting love.
takeaway: This week, set aside fifteen calm minutes with your partner and take turns: one speaks about a small concern while the other simply repeats back what they heard, says why it makes sense, and imagines how it feels, before switching roles.
summary: Harville Hendrix, a marriage therapist, asks a simple question: why do two people who fall deeply in love so often end up hurting each other? His answer is that we are not choosing partners at random. Without realising it, we are drawn to someone who carries a mix of the good and difficult qualities of the people who raised us. He calls this inner picture the imago.

According to Hendrix, a part of us hopes this new person will finally give us what we missed as children, such as attention, safety or freedom. That is why the early romantic stage feels so magical. Sooner or later, though, the same partner touches our oldest sore spots, and a power struggle begins. Each person tries to make the other change, and both feel misunderstood.

Hendrix argues that this conflict is not the end of love but the start of real work. He invites couples to build a conscious partnership, where both people understand their own wounds and agree to help heal each other's, instead of reacting on autopilot.

His best-known tool is a structured conversation often called the couples dialogue. One partner speaks while the other mirrors back what was said, then validates it by saying how it makes sense, and finally tries to imagine the feeling behind it. Slowing down like this turns arguments into understanding.

He also encourages partners to stop using quiet escape routes, such as overwork, endless screens or spending more time with friends, to avoid each other. Couples are asked to turn frustrations into specific, kind requests, and to stretch by offering the very behaviour their partner most needs, even when it feels unnatural.

Finally, Hendrix stresses deliberate kindness: regular caring gestures, small surprises and shared fun. Over time, these habits rebuild safety and warmth. Love, in his view, is not just found; it is made, day by day, by two people choosing to grow together.

questions.q: What does Hendrix mean by the 'imago'?
options: A photo album couples keep of their early dates
An unconscious inner picture of our caregivers' traits that shapes whom we are drawn to
A list of qualities we consciously want in a partner
A therapy room where couples meet
questions.why: The imago is the unconscious image, formed in childhood, that guides our attraction to a partner.

questions.q: According to the book, why does early romantic love feel so powerful?
options: Because partners have nothing in common yet
Because it is based purely on physical looks
Because part of us hopes the new partner will meet needs left unmet in childhood
Because couples rarely see each other at first
questions.why: Hendrix links the intensity of new love to the hope of finally receiving what we missed growing up.

questions.q: What stage usually follows the romantic stage in Hendrix's view?
options: The power struggle
Automatic lifelong harmony
Permanent separation
Retirement planning
questions.why: He describes a power struggle in which each partner tries to change the other.

questions.q: How does Hendrix view conflict in a committed relationship?
options: As proof the couple chose the wrong partner
As something to be hidden from each other
As a problem only professionals can solve
As an invitation to grow and heal old hurts together
questions.why: He reframes conflict as the starting point of a conscious, healing partnership.

questions.q: What are the three steps of the couples dialogue?
options: Blame, defend, apologise
Mirroring, validating and empathising
Listing, ranking and voting
Ignoring, waiting and forgetting
questions.why: The listener mirrors what was said, validates it, and then empathises with the feeling.

questions.q: In the dialogue, what does 'mirroring' involve?
options: Copying your partner's body language
Agreeing with everything your partner says
Repeating back what your partner said to show you heard it
Looking in a mirror together
questions.why: Mirroring means reflecting your partner's words back so they feel accurately heard.

questions.q: What does Hendrix mean by 'exits' in a relationship?
options: Ways partners quietly avoid closeness, such as overwork or constant screen time
Doors that should be locked at night
Legal steps toward divorce only
Planned holidays apart
questions.why: Exits are habits that drain energy away from the relationship to avoid intimacy.

questions.q: What does 'stretching' mean in the book?
options: Doing exercise together each morning
Pushing a partner to change first
Taking a long break from the relationship
Choosing to offer the behaviour your partner needs, even when it feels unnatural
questions.why: Stretching is growing beyond your comfort zone to meet your partner's needs, which also helps you grow.

questions.q: How does Hendrix suggest turning frustrations into something useful?
options: By keeping them to yourself
By turning them into specific, kind requests for change
By listing all past mistakes at once
By asking friends to take sides
questions.why: He encourages partners to express needs as clear, positive requests rather than criticism.

questions.q: Which practice does the book recommend for rebuilding warmth and safety?
options: Avoiding all disagreements
Keeping score of who gives more
Regular caring gestures, small surprises and shared fun
Spending most evenings apart
questions.why: Deliberate kindness and playfulness help couples restore a sense of safety and affection.
